draft.title: Vectors in the plane
card: A vector has a size and a direction. A scalar, such as 5 kg or 20 °C, has size only.
In the plane, a vector can be written as a column, such as (3, −2), where 3 is the move right and −2 is the move down. Here the top number is written first.
The same vector can be written with i and j components: 3i − 2j. The vector i is one unit to the right. The vector j is one unit up.
Example: the vector from A(1, 4) to B(5, 2) is found by taking end minus start. The x change is 5 − 1 = 4 and the y change is 2 − 4 = −2. So the vector is 4i − 2j.
draft.remember: A vector has size and direction. To find the vector from A to B, take B minus A.

a.q: Which vector is the same as the column vector (−4, 5), with the x part on top?
a.why: The top number is the i part and the bottom number is the j part, so (−4, 5) is −4i + 5j. The option 5i − 4j swaps the two parts, which is a common slip.
a.clue: The top number goes with i.

b.q: A drone in Geelong flies from P(6, −1) to Q(2, 3). What is the vector from P to Q?
b.why: Take end minus start: 2 − 6 = −4 and 3 − (−1) = 4, so the vector is −4i + 4j. The option 4i − 4j is start minus end, which gives the vector from Q to P.
b.clue: Subtract the start point from the end point, and take care with the −1.

problems.detail: The column vector is written inline as (3, −2), the same way the card writes the points A(1, 4) and B(5, 2). The line 'Here the top number is written first' is an awkward patch, and students may confuse a column vector with a coordinate point. Show the column stacked vertically, or say plainly that (3, −2) stands for a column with 3 on top.

check.summary: Both questions are correct, each with one right answer, and the explanations match the card. The only issue is minor: the card writes the column vector in row form like a coordinate point, which could confuse students.
